lead: Four names sit on one question: how much of what you see is real, and how much is computed. VR replaces the world. AR adds to it. MR locks the two together. XR is the family name. Exams test whether you can place a product on this map and justify the placing. The same map guides a developer choosing a display for training, retail or surgery.

blocks.text: VR (virtual reality) is a computer-generated, interactive 3D world that replaces the real one. You explore it through a tracked display, usually a head-mounted display. Tracked means the system measures your head position and orientation and updates the view from that measurement. A virtual environment is the simulated world itself: its objects, physics and coordinates.

AR (augmented reality) lays virtual content over the user's view of the real world. The view may come through a camera (video see-through) or through a see-through glass display (optical see-through). Exams use three tests. It combines real and virtual. It is registered in 3D. It is interactive in real time. Registered in 3D means a virtual object holds a fixed place relative to real objects as the camera moves. Real time means the overlay updates fast enough not to swim.

MR (mixed reality) combines real and virtual so the two share geometry. A virtual cup stands on your real desk. Your real hand passes in front and hides the cup. Anchoring to real geometry and occlusion by real geometry are the marks.

XR (extended reality) is the umbrella term for VR, AR and MR. It is not a fourth display type. A product is XR because it belongs to one of the three. Chapter 1.6 turns these tests into a side-by-side comparison.

The reality–virtuality continuum, drawn by Paul Milgram, arranges environments by how much virtual content they contain. The left end is a real environment with no virtual content. The right end is a virtual environment with no real content. AR sits near the real end: virtual added to real. Augmented virtuality sits near the virtual end: real added to virtual. VR is the right end.

Some syllabi call the two middle points 'mixed reality'. Some call the whole span 'the mixed reality spectrum'. Use the definition given in your question paper and state it. The line is not a quality scale. VR is not better than AR; each fits a different task.

The figure shows the order. Notice that AR and VR sit on one line, not on two unrelated lines. The ends of the line are the real environment (left) and the virtual environment (right); AR sits near the real end and VR at the virtual end.

The depth ladder describes how much of your senses the display takes over. Non-immersive VR uses an ordinary screen, keyboard and mouse. You see the room around the screen. Semi-immersive VR uses a large display or projection wall and some tracking. You still see part of the room. Fully immersive VR uses a head-mounted display or a room-sized projection cave and blocks the real world.

Depth is not the same as position on the continuum. A fully immersive headset can show AR if its cameras pass the real world through to your eyes. A desktop screen can show a virtual environment. The display decides depth; the content mix decides the continuum position.
A 360° video is a panorama, not a virtual environment, when your viewpoint is fixed to the recorded point and no world model responds. Dragging the view changes the look direction only.

figure.caption: Left to right, the scene goes from fully real to fully virtual: AR keeps the sofa fixed against your real wall, VR shows a cockpit with your room hidden. The 360° video from the worked example is off this line — it is a panorama on a screen, not a place on the continuum.

spec.title: Reality–virtuality continuum
spec.aria: A left-to-right line from a real environment with no virtual content, through augmented reality where a virtual sofa stays fixed on your real wall, and augmented virtuality where real content is added to virtual, to virtual reality where a cockpit is shown and your room is hidden; AR and VR are picked out.

examples.question: Classify each product as VR, AR, MR or neither. Give the reason in one line. (i) A phone shows a 3D sofa standing against your actual wall, and it stays against that wall as you walk around. (ii) A headset shows an aircraft cockpit; your room is not visible at all. (iii) A headset shows your room, and a virtual ball rolls under the real table and vanishes behind its leg. (iv) A phone plays a 360° video that you drag with your finger.
steps: Test (i): a live camera view, a virtual sofa, and the sofa stays against the actual wall as the phone moves. The overlay combines real and virtual, is registered in 3D, and responds in real time. Answer: AR.
Test (ii): the headset shows a computer-generated cockpit and your room is not visible. The real world is replaced. Answer: VR.

Test (iii): the headset shows your room and a virtual ball moves under the real table and is hidden by the real table leg. Real and virtual share geometry, and the real leg occludes the virtual ball. Answer: MR.

Test (iv): the phone plays a recorded 360° video. The viewpoint is fixed to the recorded point, there is no tracking of the room, and no virtual object is registered in 3D. Answer: neither; it is a panorama on a screen.
examples.answer: (i) AR, (ii) VR, (iii) MR, (iv) neither — a 360° video is a panorama, not VR or AR.

traps: Calling any 3D picture on a phone 'AR'. AR needs registration with the real world, in 3D, in real time.
Calling a 360° video 'VR'. VR needs a tracked viewpoint and a responsive world, not a fixed recorded panorama.
Treating MR as a synonym for AR. MR needs anchoring and occlusion by real geometry; AR needs only the three tests.
Saying XR is more immersive than VR. XR is the umbrella; VR is one member.
Forgetting the third AR test: interactive in real time. A static overlay that lags is not AR by the exam definition.

quiz.q: Define virtual reality in one sentence.
quiz.a: VR is a computer-generated, interactive 3D world that replaces the real world and is explored through a tracked display.

quiz.q: State the three tests that exams use for augmented reality.
quiz.a: It combines real and virtual; it is registered in 3D; it is interactive in real time.

quiz.q: Why is a 360° video on a phone not VR?
quiz.a: The viewpoint is fixed to the recorded point. There is no tracking of the user and no responsive 3D world model, so the real world is not replaced by an interactive simulated world.

quiz.q: A phone shows a 3D sofa against your real wall, and the sofa stays against that wall as you move the phone. Classify it and give the reason.
quiz.a: AR. The live view combines real and virtual, the sofa is registered in 3D to the real wall, and the overlay updates in real time.

quiz.q: A headset shows your room, and a virtual ball rolls under the real table and disappears behind the real table leg. Classify it and give the reason.
quiz.a: MR. The virtual ball is anchored to the real room and is occluded by real geometry.

quiz.q: What extra condition separates MR from AR in the exam definition?
quiz.a: MR requires the real and virtual content to share geometry: a virtual object is anchored to real geometry and can be hidden by real geometry. AR needs only the three tests; it may overlay content without occlusion or anchoring to a real surface.

quiz.q: Why does AR need registration in real time, not just a virtual overlay?
quiz.a: Registration keeps a virtual object at a fixed place relative to real objects. If the update is slow, the virtual object slides or swims as the camera moves, so it is no longer registered. Real-time interaction is the third test.

quiz.q: What does XR stand for, and what does it cover?
quiz.a: XR stands for extended reality. It is the umbrella term for VR, AR and MR.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, XR covers remote maintenance on factory floors, surgical rehearsal, retail try-on and safety training. Newer curricula add ethics, comfort and accessibility to the technical tests. Researchers measure registration error in millimetres and latency in milliseconds. Search for Milgram's continuum, SLAM, optical see-through and occlusion in AR.
